summary_grc: ὁ Ἀκρίσιος τὸν χρησμὸν δείσας τὴν θυγατέρα ἐν θαλάμῳ χαλκῷ φρουρεῖ· ὕστερον δὲ αὐτὴν μετὰ τοῦ Περσέως εἰς λάρνακα βαλὼν εἰς τὴν θάλατταν ῥίπτει.
summary_en: Elpis asks for a story about the sea. Kleinias tells of an oracle, a bronze chamber, a shower of gold, a mother and baby set adrift in a chest, and the task that sent Perseus after the Gorgon's head. Adapted from Apollodorus 2.4.1–2.
caption_grc: τὴν θυγατέρα μετὰ τοῦ παιδὸς εἰς λάρνακα βαλὼν εἰς τὴν θάλατταν ἔρριψεν.

original.note: Apollodorus, Library 2.4.1–2 (to Polydectes' demand), adapted in paragraphs 1–3; the last lines of the story, the Gorgon and the end of the oracle, summarise the rest of 2.4.2–4. Apollodorus wrote in the 1st or 2nd century AD. He gives two versions of how Danae became pregnant: watch for ὡς ἔνιοι λέγουσιν … ὡς δὲ ἔνιοί φασι.

«ὁ δὲ Ἀκρίσιος οὐκ ἐπίστευεν ὅτι ὁ παῖς τοῦ Διὸς ἦν. αὐτὸς μὲν οὐκ ἀπέκτεινεν αὐτούς·»

«Πολυδέκτης δέ, ὁ τῆς νήσου βασιλεύς, τῆς Δανάης ἤρα· ὁ δὲ Περσεὺς νεανίας ἤδη ἦν καὶ τὴν μητέρα ἐφρούρει.»

glosses.value: the Gorgons: three winged sisters with snakes for hair; only Medusa could die (Apollodorus 2.4.2)

sentences.text: «ὁ δὲ Ἑρμῆς καὶ ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ σύμμαχοι τῷ Περσεῖ ἦσαν. πτερωτὰ οὖν πέδιλα ἔχων πρὸς τὰς Γοργόνας ἐπέτετο.»
«καὶ εἰς ἀσπίδα χαλκῆν ὁρῶν, οὐκ εἰς τὴν Γοργόνα, τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτῆς ἀπέτεμεν, καὶ πετόμενος οἴκαδε ἐκόμισεν.»

τὸ μαντεῖον: the oracle · τὸ ἐν Δελφοῖς μαντεῖον

notice: ὁ δὲ θεὸς ἔφη παῖδα ἐκ τῆς θυγατρὸς γενήσεσθαι, ὃς αὐτὸν ἀποκτενεῖ
ὡς μὲν ἔνιοι λέγουσιν … ὡς δὲ ἔνιοί φασιν …
τοῦτον δὲ τὸν χρησμὸν δείσας ὁ Ἀκρίσιος … τὴν Δανάην ἐφρούρει
Apollodorus: μὴ πιστεύσας ὑπὸ Διὸς ἐφθάρθαι

grammar.md:
**Oracles and other people's words.** Myths are full of prophecies and of versions. Apollodorus reports both with the constructions you learned in Units 8–9.

**1. What the god said: φημί + infinitive.** ὁ θεὸς ἔφη παῖδα … γενήσεσθαι 'the god said that a child would be born'. The subject of the infinitive is in the accusative (παῖδα); the tense of the infinitive keeps the tense of the prophecy (future γενήσεσθαι). Apollodorus himself writes γενέσθαι (aorist): later Greek often uses the aorist infinitive where Attic prose prefers the future after verbs of saying.

**2. The relative clause that looks ahead.** … παῖδα, ὃς αὐτὸν ἀποκτενεῖ 'a child who will kill him'. A relative with the future often carries the doom of a myth.

**3. Versions: ὡς ἔνιοι λέγουσιν / ὡς ἔνιοί φασι.** 'as some say'. Apollodorus sets two stories side by side with μέν … δέ and does not choose. Notice the accent: ἔνιοί φασι. An enclitic after a word accented on the third syllable from the end adds an acute to that word's last syllable (ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν).

**4. μή with a participle.** Apollodorus writes μὴ πιστεύσας 'not believing'. Attic normally negates a plain participle with οὐ (οὐ πιστεύσας); later Greek uses μή more and more. Read both the same way.

| Apollodorus | our adaptation | Attic habit |
|---|---|---|
| ἔφη γενέσθαι παῖδα | ἔφη παῖδα γενήσεσθαι | future infinitive for a future event |
| χάλκεον | χαλκοῦν | contracted adjective |
| θάλασσαν | θάλατταν | Attic -ττ- |
| μὴ πιστεύσας | οὐκ ἐπίστευεν | οὐ with a statement of fact |

culture.title: Oracles: asking the gods
culture.md:
Akrisios does what real Greeks did: he sends to **Delphi**. At Apollo's sanctuary on the slopes of Parnassus a priestess, the **Pythia**, answered questions in the god's name, and cities and private people consulted her for centuries (Delphi was active from at least the 8th century BC until the late 4th century AD). Questions were about colonies, wars, marriages, children and harvests; many surviving answers are practical ('sacrifice to this god'), and the riddling, double-edged oracle is more at home in stories than in the records.

In myth an oracle almost always comes true, and trying to avoid it is what makes it come true: Akrisios locks up his daughter, Laios exposes the baby Oedipus, and both are killed by the child. The Athenian audience of 431 knew the pattern well from tragedy; Sophocles' *Oedipus the King* was probably staged within a few years of our story.

The image of Danae and the infant Perseus in the chest was a favourite of Athenian vase painters of the early 5th century: Akrisios stands by, a carpenter finishes the chest, and Danae holds the baby as she steps in. Oracles were serious business in Athens too: in the story of 432–430, oracle-mongers (χρησμολόγοι) sang old prophecies in the streets as the war began (Thucydides 2.8, 2.21).
